summary: Movement is told by the verb and a preposition with the genitive: إِلَى answers “where to?” (أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ), مِنْ answers “where from?” (أَعُودُ مِنَ الْعَمَلِ), and بِـ gives the means of transport (أُسَافِرُ بِالْقِطَارِ, by train) — but “on foot” is the adverb مَشْيًا, with no preposition. The questions are إِلَى أَيْنَ؟ (where to?), مِنْ أَيْنَ؟ (where from?) and كَيْفَ؟ (how?). A few verbs take the place directly as an object: دَخَلَ الْبَيْتَ (enter the house), غَادَرَ الْمَدِينَةَ (leave the town), وَصَلَ الْمَدِينَةَ or وَصَلَ إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ (reach the town). Arabic has one verb for going, however you go (ذَهَبَ = German gehen and fahren), and the case never depends on “where” or “where to”: after any preposition the noun is genitive. The movement verbs include the most irregular verbs of the language — hollow (قَادَ / يَقُودُ, عَادَ / يَعُودُ, جَاءَ / يَجِيءُ), with a weak last letter (مَشَى / يَمْشِي, بَقِيَ / يَبْقَى) and assimilated (وَصَلَ / يَصِلُ): learn them with their present.

blocks.title: Not فِي for “to”.
blocks.text: Greek σε and German in / zu cover both “at” and “to”; Arabic separates them: فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ (at school) but إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ (to school).

blocks.title: By bus, by car: بِـ with the article.
blocks.text: بِالْحَافِلَةِ, بِالْقِطَارِ, بِالطَّائِرَةِ, بِالسَّيَّارَةِ, بِالدَّرَّاجَةِ — and for a taxi بِسَيَّارَةِ أُجْرَةٍ. مَعَ is company (مَعَ أَخِي), never the vehicle.

blocks.title: One “go” for all.
blocks.text: German says gehen on foot and fahren by vehicle, Hebrew הָלַךְ and נָסַע; Arabic uses ذَهَبَ for both and adds the vehicle: ذَهَبْتُ بِالْقِطَارِ, ذَهَبْتُ مَشْيًا. “Drive (a car)” is قَادَ السَّيَّارَةَ.

German changes the case with the direction (in der Schule — where? dative; in die Schule — where to? accusative). Arabic changes the preposition instead and keeps the genitive: فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ, إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ, مِنَ الْمَدْرَسَةِ.

askYourself: Is there movement? Towards a place → إِلَى; away from a place, or the origin → مِنْ (مِنَ before al-); no movement → فِي.
How? By a vehicle → بِـ + al- (بِالْقِطَارِ); on foot → مَشْيًا.
Does the verb take the place directly? دَخَلَ, غَادَرَ (and وَصَلَ, اِنْتَظَرَ) — then no preposition.
Is the noun after the preposition genitive (-i, -in)?
Which present has this verb? Hollow يَقُودُ / يَعُودُ / يَجِيءُ, weak يَمْشِي / يَبْقَى, assimilated يَصِلُ, form III يُسَافِرُ / يُغَادِرُ.
Asking? إِلَى أَيْنَ؟ (where to?), مِنْ أَيْنَ؟ (where from?), كَيْفَ؟ (how?).

traps: *أُسَافِرُ مَعَ الْقِطَارِ → أُسَافِرُ بِالْقِطَارِ (مَعَ is “together with” a person).
“On foot” has no بِـ: أَذْهَبُ مَشْيًا.
*دَخَلْتُ فِي الْبَيْتِ → دَخَلْتُ الْبَيْتَ (or دَخَلْتُ إِلَى الْبَيْتِ).
*غَادَرْتُ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ → غَادَرْتُ الْبَيْتَ (غَادَرَ takes an object); but خَرَجْتُ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ.
The w of وَصَلَ disappears in the present: يَصِلُ, not *يَوْصِلُ.
بَقِيَ has i in the past and a in the present: يَبْقَى; “they stay” is يَبْقَوْنَ.

quiz.why: Movement towards a place: إِلَى + genitive.
The means of transport takes بِـ with the article.

quiz.q: “He walks to work” (on foot) — which is right?
quiz.why: مَشْيًا is an adverb: no preposition.
مِنْ becomes مِنَ before al-, and the noun is genitive.
وَصَلَ is assimilated: the w drops in the present.
دَخَلَ takes the place as a direct object; its present vowel is u.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew has the same three helpers — לְ / אֶל (to), מִ / מִן (from), בְּ (by: בָּאוֹטוֹבּוּס) — but, like German, it separates הָלַךְ (go on foot) and נָסַע (go by vehicle); Arabic says ذَهَبَ for both.
German: gehen on foot, fahren by vehicle; nach / zu / in + accusative for “where to”, aus / von + dative for “where from”, mit dem Bus. Arabic: one ذَهَبَ, إِلَى / مِنْ / بِـ, always the genitive.
Chinese puts the direction in the verb (去 go, 来 come) and the vehicle before it: 我坐公共汽车去学校; “from … to …” is 从 … 到 …. Arabic: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ بِالْحَافِلَةِ.
إِلَى, مِنْ and بِـ were met in lesson 11; here they move.
Commands with the same verbs: اِذْهَبْ!, تَعَالَ!, اُدْخُلْ!
